abstract: Recent research on Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) has focused on learning from language, visual, and acoustic modalities with incomplete data to infer human sentiment. Most studies typically compensate for missing information by reconstructing modality features or designing complicated fusion mechanisms. However, these methods still suffer from spurious generation and noisy guidance due to the lack of high-level semantic grounding in partially observed multimodal evidence. To address these issues, we propose SemMSA, a latent semantic-aided framework that constructs rich sentiment-relevant semantics with LLMs, fully integrating with all modalities via anchor-free spectral alignment. It mainly consists of Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) and Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA). Specifically, CSR first adaptively extracts visual and acoustic representations by corresponding adapters to form a unified multimodal prefix with language in the frozen LLM embedding space. It then iteratively produces continuous discriminative semantic states through a token-efficient latent refinement process without decoding explicit text. Next, CSA simultaneously aligns the refined semantics with all modalities by enhancing the dominant spectral component of their kernel Gram matrix. This captures global nonlinear dependencies among all representations without relying on a predefined anchor modality. In addition, an instance-level spectral separation constraint preserves cross-sample discriminability and mitigates representation collapse. Extensive experiments on SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that SemMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/SemMSA/.

sections.body: Missing visual and acoustic data is common, and reconstruction methods recover low-level features rather than sentiment semantics. Fusion methods may overfit modality co-occurrence patterns seen in training. The authors propose SemMSA, which uses Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) to map visual and acoustic features through adapters into the frozen LLM embedding space. CSR then refines continuous latent semantic states without decoding text. Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA) aligns semantic, language, visual, and acoustic representations through a kernel Gram matrix, without a predefined anchor modality. The introduction claims an accuracy improvement of 1.4% on average under diverse missingness.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Incomplete multimodal sentiment data calls for high-level semantics, which SemMSA supplies from a frozen LLM without decoding text.

sections.body: The review groups prior work into fusion methods, including dominance-guided approaches such as LNLN and P-RMF, and reconstruction methods, including diffusion-based recovery. The authors argue that reconstruction recovers superficial statistical patterns rather than sentiment cues, and that diffusion models incur substantial computational costs. Pairwise contrastive alignment ties each representation to a single anchor, which the authors say misses global structure among modalities. The Gram matrix has appeared in theoretical analyses and other tasks. The authors state that, to their knowledge, this is the first use of LLMs for semantic-level compensation in MSA.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior methods reconstruct or fuse missing modalities, or align pairs to an anchor, and the authors say none uses LLM semantics for MSA.

sections.body: Each modality is encoded by frozen encoders into a sequence $\mathbf{X}_{m}$ in the original text notation. Visual and acoustic adapters use $M$ learnable prompts and $B$ blocks to map features into the LLM embedding space, and language is embedded by the LLM. The concatenated prefix is refined over $O$ steps: at each step the last hidden state is appended as a continuous token, and the resulting states are pooled into one semantic vector without text decoding. CSA builds a kernel Gram matrix of normalized semantic, visual, acoustic, and language representations using an RBF kernel. A loss on the largest eigenvalue pushes the matrix toward rank one, and an instance-level separation term penalizes similarity between dominant directions of different samples.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: SemMSA refines frozen-LLM hidden states into latent semantics and aligns all four representations through a kernel Gram matrix's dominant spectral component.

sections.body: Experiments use MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS, with test missing rates from 0.0 to 0.9. Training uses a 200-epoch schedule and Qwen3-1.7B as the frozen LLM. On MOSI, SemMSA reports Acc-5 of 40.93 and MAE of 1.011, and the text says its Acc-5 improves on the best baseline, TF-Mamba, by 2.43%. On MOSEI it reports Acc-2 of 79.61 and F1 of 80.62. On SIMS the text says it surpasses P-RMF by 0.087 in Corr. Under inter-modal missingness, Table 3 reports an average F1 of 77.89, which the text says is 2.71% above CorrKD. The authors attribute these gains to semantic compensation and spectral alignment.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: SemMSA posts the strongest averaged results against all listed baselines under intra-modal missingness on MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the two components. CSR maps visual and acoustic features into the frozen LLM space and produces sentiment-relevant latent semantics through hidden-state refinement without decoding text. CSA jointly aligns semantic, language, visual, and acoustic representations by enhancing the dominant spectral component of their kernel Gram matrix, and adds instance-level spectral separation. The authors state that these capture global nonlinear cross-modal dependencies without an anchor modality. They claim the method is effective on SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI under diverse missing-modality settings. No new experiments are reported in this section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion restates the two modules and claims effectiveness across SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI under missing-modality settings.

sections.body: The appendix gives Algorithm 1, which extracts features, applies adapters, runs CSR and CSA, adds a separation loss, and fuses representations for prediction. The theory section shows that a rank-one kernel Gram matrix is equivalent to full kernelized alignment (Lemma 1), and that increasing the dominant eigenvalue reduces residual spectral energy (Theorem 1). It states that the alignment direction comes from all modalities rather than an anchor, and that the separation loss prevents instances from collapsing to one direction. Stated limitations: evaluation covers only MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS; the latent semantics are less interpretable than text; and alignment may suffer when most modality cues are unreliable. The societal impact section lists privacy, demographic bias, and high-stakes misuse risks.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the training algorithm, spectral alignment theory, extra results, a case study, limitations, and societal impact.
